Review from a Phasmophobia Veteran with 600+ hours

This game runs superbly with unreal engine backing it. Solid 60+ FPS. TONS of assets being used on each map. TONS of events that you'll never see coming. Lets not beat around the bush, everyone wants to do the age old "is this the killer of said game". This games on a entirely different level, you exorcise the paranormal which already is different. It has things in it Phasmo can only dream of. You enter the house to find spooky stuff thru the ENTIRE HOUSE, NOT just where the ghost is. Events happen thru the ENTIRE MAP, YOU are the one who has to narrow it down. The game already has MORE ghosts then ANY OTHER GAME after years of them being out. And already the dev's are hard at work patch day after day of adding, fixing, etc.

Which again, since people like to compare? Phasmo updates have months between them. Its the same old, same old go in, find ghost, figure out what it is, and leave. Boring, repetitive.

This game you can go into a map you've been on 6+ times and some new event happens to you that you thought you'd seen/experienced them all. You have DOZENS of ghosts to pick thru of who, what, when, where, and why. And the maps themselves are actually places that LOOK and FEEL haunted. They aren't new, shiny, just bought from the store maps/places. 

If you die, and yes you'll die. You actually get to help as a ghost. You aren't punished for maybe bad luck, really difficult ghost, etc. You can still be in the game, without being among the living.

The game has ALOT of potential. The game also has a system of rewarding you already via playing by actually buying new locations to go and live at, yes, no longer living in your mom's garage. You can actually have a home, pub, light house, and more! You can change the aesthetics of your place too! And buy things for your character to wear. You can even have PETS live in your home that actively move around the home doing their own thing! The game FEELS more alive, because it is. And the potential is limitless with the new unreal engine these dev's are using. 

And got a bad player in your lobby? There is a kick button for the host. Something phasmo STILL AFTER YEARS has not implemented where you & others can game with piece of mind that if someones a bad sport, clown, griefer, etc? You can BAM get rid of them.

Oh and roadmap? You don't have to go to trello to hope the dev delivers on their promise. There is a big huge map system of showing of current maps you have, future maps, and how many maps to come. Discord isn't overrun by a tyrant either, nor bad sports. They actively encourage suggestions, feedback, etc. They don't just ignore the discord and let mods run rampant of taking advantage of players to cause a huge drama issue, where their streamer pals who play with them will swing in and save/defend the game cause it'll cost them revenue and its their job. (if you know, you know) Thats a huge plus too :)

Final thoughts? Is this the phasmo killer? Heard that alot playing WoW for 15+ years. No phasmo is doing that to itself. Play this game on its own merits if you enjoy a ghost hunting, ghost exorcising, spooky experience. With limitless potential of unreal engine behind it, dev's and a community with actual passion & love for the game already.

And PS - if incase you aren't running a top of the line graphics card (above a 2060 pretty much). Turn off motion blur, shadows down to medium/low and you'll have a wonderful experience with no real issues.

Hope to see you all in the game! PEACE!

Initially, I brushed this off as another Phasmophobia clone. But after delving deeper, it felt more like Phasmophobia's edgier, younger cousin who's practicing dark arts in the basement.

While the game unmistakably draws inspiration from Phasmophobia, especially in terms of equipment and the ghost-hunting premise, it offers a unique twist. Instead of just identifying the ghost, you're tasked with sending it back to where it came from. Discover its identity, complete objectives, and then banish the pesky spirit.

Total Score: 8.8/10

Graphics/Visuals (8/10):

While the graphics are fairly average, the visuals are commendable. They elevate the overall ambiance, immersing the player further into the eerie setting.

Sound & Music (9/10):

This game will give you genuine chills, and the impeccable sound design plays a pivotal role in that. It doesn't just enhance the atmosphere; it creates it.

Story & Narrative (9/10):

While there isn't a traditional story, the ambiance generated in each map tells a tale of its own, making each session distinct.

Gameplay & Mechanics (9/10):

The thrill of fleeing from a ghost is somewhat dampened when your character appears to have a strong aversion to physical exertion. Some mechanics might be irksome, but they've been intentionally integrated to intensify the overall experience. Each tool and instrument is thoughtfully incorporated.

Replayability & Content (8.5/10):

It's the kind of game you'd dive into intermittently, with every return bringing a fresh sense of dread. While the developers have introduced some new content, the game could benefit from an expanded map variety. Incorporating a workshop-style feature might very well give it an upper hand in the genre.

Innovation & Originality (8/10):

Despite its distinct approach, certain elements are unmistakably reminiscent of Phasmophobia, albeit with a twist. Nevertheless, it does present a refreshing perspective on the genre.

Technical Performance & Optimization:

On my rig with a 3080, the game runs mostly smooth, save for the occasional hiccup.

Value (10/10):

At $15 USD, it's a steal. The gameplay experience it offers at this price point is unbeatable.

Final Thoughts:

This isn't just another ghost-hunting game. It's a thrilling adventure that takes a familiar formula and dares to innovate, albeit with varying degrees of success. Whether you're a veteran of the genre or a curious newcomer, this game promises a chilling experience that's worth every cent.

A review from the viewpoint of a casual Phasmophobia fan, hours accumulated mainly from playing with friend groups consisting of 3 or 4. 

The Pros: (4/5/2023)
- Game stomps Phasmophobia when it comes to graphical differences, if this is what the next gen of PC games has to offer then sign me up. 
- Spook variety, Phasmophobia has a handful of scares that can get very repetitive and eventually allows most of the playerbase to become desensitized to the content and eventually rarely get scared when activity is present.
- Environment/atmosphere is an upgrade, even though the first handful of hours are gonna be spent hunting ghouls in the same abandoned house until level 3 is met you can tell that every map that IS included in this current build has been carefully planned and executes a perfectly spooky experience. 
- Unique take on the plethora of Phasmophobia clones, the objective system relies on you finishing the sequence as follows, identify the ghost type, optional objectives, exorcise the ghost.
- Customization, though I haven't really explored the safe house customization it does seem fairly fleshed out for early access and is a nice addition. Character customization is barebones but understandable for early access.


The Cons: (4/5/2023)
- The game just released too early IMO, I can see this taking off to high popularity even rivaling Phasmophobia being the next house name game but at this point in time, the lack of maps will turn a lot of players off.
- Voice recognizing commands is very barebones as of right now, when it comes to ouji board commands and getting responses from the spirit box is very basic of now but I am sure devs will expand on this in the future. 
- Progression is VERY slow, though it has the potential to snowball. Players will understandably complain and review negative about the slow progression experiencing the grind to level 1 to 3 is painful considering equipment is outrageously expensive considering the beginner gear doesn't allow you to finish all objectives/ optional objectives. However you can speed leveling up once you get the photo camera and candle. 
- I found the 15 dollar price tag completely reasonable for the quality of game that I received, but I can see it being 5 dollars too much for a lot of the average Steam user, 10 dollars would probably entice trying the game out more for a bigger playerbase. But thats what steam sales are for anyway. 

My rating: 7.8/10

This game is fantastic! one of my favorites in my library. If you are someone who is interested in this game because you love or loved phasmophobia I strongly urge you to pick up this game. I personally think this game is better in almost every way. minus a few things, but this game has only been out a year so i think with more time it could just all around be the better game. I have over 300 hours in phas and almost 80 in this game at the time of writing this. I think it is important to lay out what i think this game does better.

Things demo does better:
1) The maps are not only designed better, they are also scarier than phas in my opinion. They also come out much more frequently than Phas maps, instead of just making U.I. changes over and over again.
2) The side objectives CLEAR Phas's they are much more detailed and engaging, and rarely end up in someone dying for absolutely no good reason. reading notes about the games lore and actually accomplishing things is just way more immersive in my opinion.
3) You can actually exorcise the ghost. I always thought it was strange in phas how you just figure out what type of ghost it is then you leave. again it makes Phas feel less complete and less engaging.
4) You can customize your character, change your hub world, and have a pet. with the hub world interacting with the story at times. nothing crazy but i think just adds another layer to the game that Phas just does not have.
5) that brings me to my next point which i feel is more subjective, but I love the fact that this game has a overarching story and all the maps have lore behind them it adds depth to the things going on around you.
6)ghost events. This is a big one that demo just sweeps with. i have played a decent amount of both games, and most ghost events play out the exact same way in phas where as here im still seeing the ghost do things ive never seen before on the regular. it really keeps you on your toes. I believe this to be a unity restriction on phas's part i may be wrong but this game is just way scarier. I often am not scared by phas sometimes even downright falling asleep waiting for anything to happen. where as in demo I am on the regular in the middle of a mental breakdown this game can be terrifying at times. phas is more of a slow burn that just mildly creeps me out every once and a little while.

Things Phas does better:
1) Having three tiers of equipment. I think which game has better equipment is down to personal preference, but i do find myself wishing demo had different tiers of equipment to unlock like phas.
2) The proximity chat is WAY better in Phas. Demo doesn't have a radio even so i think this game is best played in a discord call, because the ghost can always hear you no matter what unlike phas where you have to actually talk through game chat to be heard.
3) Activity meter this one is not only helpful on Phas but it add another layer of depth for whoever decides to be the truck (or in this game the tent) guy. Although you can look at different cameras in this game which is something i wish phas would do, but overall i still think the truck is more engaging in phas because of things like D.O.T.S and spirit orbs. In demo you are really just looking for ESG and Easel. altough that does mean you are inside the house more often being scared so I will let you decide if that is a positive or not. It is for me because I play these games to get scared and sometimes truck duty puts me to sleep.
4) Basketball. 

I don't mean to sound like I'm knocking Phas, Because i still like it, but I would be lying if i didn't say this game has more of my attention. Phas was my first PC game after I built my computer and this game would't even exist without it, but if you are on the fence about getting this game i say go for it. I really do not think you will be disappointed out of all my friends we all play phas and demo on a regular basis and 5 out of 6 enjoy this game more. I genuinely can not recommend this game enough, This is definitely the longest review i have ever written for anything. Thank you for coming to my ted talk and happy hunting!

This game was fun for a few hours. However, there are bugs that shouldn't exist in a full release game, such as having to recreate the lobby every time you finish a game, and a footpath that pings you around as you traverse it on the Bedlam Asylum map.

The game has many missing features that other games of the same genre already have, like saving a difficulty preset, auto buying lost equipment and daily/ weekly tasks (these are promised on the store page, I do not see any trace of them in game). 

The gameplay is fun for the first couple of exorcisms, after that it becomes stale. The jump scares are scripted, the ghosts are not difficult to guess as the abilities they use are not rare, even the difficulty modifiers don't make the game hard. Having custom modifiers to make the game as hard as possible just made it easier to get enough money and xp for everything as there was still no challenge, just inflated rewards. 

Visually the game is deceiving it's portrayed on the store page to be stunning and immersive, although that is not the case. After playing the first few maps which I did enjoy, I reached the hospital map, I generally enjoy the larger, creepier maps in these games so I was quite excited, except walking around the decor was lazy, things placed in areas they don't belong, other items copy pasted as clutter and it hit me that the game is an Unreal engine asset flip. The hospital map can be found as a full free map on the unreal engine asset library, almost everything in the game is from a free asset pack. It's very poorly developed overall, nothing is polished just copy pasted and sold as a game. After the realisation the only reason to play was to get 100% achievements so I can uninstall it.

Currently, I recommend this game, but, there are definitely some issues.

First off, this type of game is not new at this point. Phasmophobia started it all and now we have dozens of these... Most people who actually play these types of games now are veterans. We know what we're doing. That being said:

The way everything is capped per level is kind of ridiculous. Having to grind the exact same level at least half a dozen times before being able to level up high enough to unlock another map is annoying. Nobody wants to be forced to play the same map over and over and over again just to grind though for experience; especially when you may or may not have all of the equipment to accomplish the optional objectives in able to actually fully complete a game for the full payoff.

Depending on that, it could take more than 4-5 play-throughs just to level up one time..... Dude, that's insane.

Also, the cost of many items is honestly just laughable..... Salt, in any country and any age would NEVER cost over $1000.... Put some realistic costs to items in this game, and make the cost/pay scale more balanced. We shouldn't have to spend half of our money getting basic items that we lose every time we die, it's absurd.

Lastly..... don't make us only able to play on easy difficulty until we reach level 5, that's  boring and annoying for veterans who have played 3,4 + types of these games for years.... It's not a good way to retain players who don't want to wait 20 minutes for stuff to start happening...

Other than this, the game is a 10/10 for atmospherics, graphics, map uniqueness, mechanics and everything else. The game has real potential, but stop locking everything down so hard. This isn't a competitive game! It's a co-op game!

I used to love this game, but that was before the 2.0 update.

The 2.0 update introduced Nvidia's ray tracing into the game and the developer decided not to let people turn it off.

This made the game literally unplayable for anyone who doesn't have a high end modern GeForce or a bleeding edge Radeon card even though the game ran perfectly fine before. This isn't the general hyperbole of "This game's unplayable because it runs under some arbitrary number of frames per second so it's unplayable" that you generally see in reviews or forums.

This is "the game crashes to desktop if your card can't do ray tracing extremely well."

If you force the game into running DirectX 11 so it will even get past the splash screens then you're met with a situation where you can see light sources but nothing is illuminated. The floors are black, the walls are black, the tables and chairs are black, There's no ambient light and no amount of gamma correction will offset this.

There have been multiple threads in the forums complaining about this and asking for a way to switch ray tracing off or even just asking for some direct comment which have been met with silence because they seem to only respond to comments in their discord channel. Which the link to has been broken at least since the release of the 2.0 update if not before.

I hate leaving this as my review because the game before this was excellent. It had fantastic atmosphere, it's take on the ghost hunting tools was interesting, most of the gameplay mechanics were functional (if a bit slow sometimes,) But the decision to, more than two years after release, change the technical requirement specifications to something that requires a much higher specification GPU literally overnight makes me have to give it a "not recommended" unless or until they make ray tracing optional.

Edit: To correct one thing I'd been missing, it turns out there is a functional link to their discord server in one place of the community section. However the one in the discussion boards that is pinned where they literally tell you to go for support or reporting is still broken at last check. This in no way changes the substance of the complaints.

Let me be clear: this is a decent game with a lot of potential. The reason that I'm giving it a thumbs down simply has to do with the method by which they scare you, and how that ties in with the replayability. 

This game gets compared a LOT to Phasmophobia for obvious reasons, and to me this game is superior to Phasmo... for the first few hours. After that, it starts to get really old really fast. I don't think that this is a bad game per se, and I want to avoid comparing it to Phasmo for the rest of the review. The fundamental issue with this game is that it is designed to be replayed many times over but the scares are heavily scripted. To be fair, the scares are VERY good. Whoever designed this game absolutely nails horror, from the atmosphere to the jumpscares. However, once you've seen each scare (and there are only so many on each map), then the game completely loses its effect. This combined with a limited amount of maps makes the game feel stagnant after only a few hours.

I also cannot understand why the heck you need to level up in order to unlock each map. To me this is a very bizarre choice and it makes the game feel unnecessarily grindy and locks out less patient players from the full experience. While not a problem to me personally, I had a few friends give up on this game because leveling up to get to all of the maps seemed like too great of a chore. I'm sure that the payoff is fine, but I can completely understand their POV because when you are strictly limited to playing only a few maps, and each map has a very limited subset of scripted jumpscares, then it feels boring and tedious, not like adrenaline-pumping horror.

[h1]Demonoligist: Full Review[/h1]

So Demonoligist can be seen as a "Phasmophobia Clone" to quite a lot of people, however there are some things that it improves on and adds to the experience. Things I wanted from Phasmophobia from the start. The investigations are extremely similar compared to Phasmophobia but it takes the whole "retro" look when it comes to some of your tools.

[h1]What I love about Demonoligist compared to Phasmophobia:[/h1]
> Better jumpscares, although some ghost events are scripted it has better jumpscares overall.
> Exorcism after investigation. This is the thing I really love about Demonologist, because as opposed to Phasmophobia you actually do something about the haunting. In Phas you just investigate and leave the people to deal with the ghost "Yeah bro your house is haunted, but at least you know what ghost is haunting it." Demonologist allows you to exorcise the ghost after you completed the investigation which adds another level of enjoyment.
> Environments are more "spooky" which is amazing, in Phas its just some random persons house or cabin.
> Tools are straight forward. You can read the tooltips on what each tool does but its easier to get used to compared to the large variety of tools Phas has. Some might see the large quantity of tools as a bonus, but I always found it annoying, running back and forth with each tool trying to find what the hell was needed. Demonologist has fewer tools allowing for a smoother experience and less back tracking.
> Ghost noises and environmental interactions when it comes to haunting ramps up quite a lot in Demonologist, where as Phasmophobia has fewer interactions and more frequent haunts which doesn't build the same tension that Demonologist does.
> One key interactions. The whole dragging to open doors annoyed me so much in Phas and could sometimes break during a ghost chase where with Demonologist its a simple E for interact which is such a relief.
> Hidey spots. In Phasmophobia the closets or some of the rooms offer no "real" protection where with Demonologist the closets have saved me... Not so much my friend but thats a him problem.
> Character customisation. I know it's very basic but just being able to customise my character is such a nice addition.

[h1]What I don't like:[/h1]
> Low sprint. I get that you try to build tension and want to add a level of "spook" to the game, but I am not playing a morbidly obese man that can't sprint for more than 5 seconds without becoming exhausted. Phasmo has the same issue.
> XP gain is a bit slow as well as money, but the higher the difficulty the greater the reward I suppose. It just becomes a problem when you need to do the same map 3 or 4 times before unlocking the next one.
> I had a bug where the side objective wouldn't complete even though I interacted with all the crucifixes. This kind of forced me to finish the "hunt" sooner, losing out on extra xp. But now I'm nitpicking.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Phasmophobia has had three years to build up to what it is now. Demonologist is still in its infancy, but the fact that it has features in which should have been in Phasmo years ago now speaks volume to the developers commitment. I look forward to the future of Demonologist and what it could bring to the table. This game has replaced Phasmo for me completely. So if you are wondering which one you should get, Demo or Phasmo, I would recommend Demo simply because it has features in it that improve on Phasmo so much. I know I haven't invested a lot of time in the game as of yet, but believe me when I say that this is just the beginning for me.

I've played Phasmaphobia (P) and Demonologist (D), and here is my quick comparison review. Demonologist is the better game. Both have similarities - UI, graphics, ghosts, discretionary objectives, sanity level (health bar), tools to discern ghosts, and I could probably go on. The key differences that make Demonologist better - D has better UI (something as simple as opening and closing the door), scare factor goes to D (there's more in your face and ad-hoc occurrences in D than in P), feeling of accomplishment goes to D (The simple fact that you can exorcise a demon in D and cannot in P is HUGE! There's something so satisfying about unloading a salt shotgun on a ghost trying to kill you), ghost selection is better in P (you're not penalized and stuck with your selection in P but if you pick wrong in D there's no turning back), and map selection goes to P (P has been out longer so you have a great selection of different maps to try versus D atm). Some common gripes about both games: 1) Tools do not work 100% of the time and you're left deducing (while this might be intended, sometimes you'll encounter a ghost where none of the clues are easy to find and you're left guessing), 2) Running needs some tweaking - I get what they're trying to do, but keep it a bit more realistic instead of running like we're 100 years old, and 3) Not really a gripe but a wish that we could have more than 4 players.
After 10+ hrs of Demonologist, I can finally perform an exorsism at my home. Thank you.

Among the many Phasmophobia clones, Demonologist stands out by carving out its own identity, specifically, as a scarier alternative. Compared to Phasmophobia, this game boasts better graphics and excels in creating an eerie atmosphere. One of its biggest strengths is its haunted house environments, filled with small details and Easter eggs that make each map feel immersive. Where Phasmophobia’s maps often resemble ordinary locations with the lights off, Demonologist feels like stepping into a full-fledged horror movie, complete with randomized jump scares that keep each playthrough feeling fresh.

One of the game’s best features is its exorcism mechanic, which adds a more satisfying goal beyond simply identifying the ghost. Since exorcisms can only be performed after correctly guessing the ghost type, often when your sanity is already low, you have to decide whether to risk it for the extra reward or play it safe and leave. These exorcisms vary by map, making it fun to learn how to complete each one.

However, Demonologist does have areas that need improvement. A major issue is persistent problems with microphone recognition. While this didn’t affect me too often, there were times when the game inexplicably stopped recognizing my mic. In a social, party-style game like this, proximity chat is crucial for immersion. Losing the ability to talk to the ghost, an important mechanic for gathering evidence, can be particularly frustrating.

The hunting mechanics also have some flaws. Hiding from ghosts can feel inconsistent, as they sometimes spot you entering a hiding place when it seems like they shouldn’t. Additionally, surviving a hunt often boils down to simply using a protective item or waiting in a hiding spot for 30 seconds, which can get tedious. Worse, ghosts sometimes chain hunt, repeatedly locking the exit door and forcing you to scramble back to your hiding spot over and over.

Another point of criticism is the game's approach to ghost behavior. In Phasmophobia, experienced players can identify ghosts based on unique traits and behaviors beyond just gathering evidence. While Demonologist does give ghosts some distinctive behaviors, they aren’t designed in a way that makes them reliably identifiable without traditional evidence. This limits progression, after playing for long enough and learning all the jump scares, the game starts to feel like a waiting game until new content drops. That said, the developers have done a solid job of adding updates so far.

While Demonologist can be played solo, it truly shines when experienced with friends.

Final Verdict: 7/10

Following the deeply disappointing *Haunt Chaser*, which left me with a bitter taste in my mouth, Clock Wizard is giving the co-op horror genre another go.

This time round, we’re once again faced with a *Phasmophobia*-style game… but is that all there is to it?

Just like Phasmophobia, the rules are simple: you must identify a ghost in a specific location, find the room it haunts, uncover various clues using different objects and finally… survive.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2975670188

Nothing out of the ordinary so far, you might say. And you’d be right.

Where Demonologist really stands out is in the game’s overall atmosphere. Forget about houses that look like basic 3D models; here we have fewer maps, but they’re far more detailed and visually appealing (well, everything’s relative – the textures are sometimes truly awful).
On top of that, there are various scripted events in each map: spawns, moving furniture. You get used to it in the end, but it adds a bit more spice to the overall gameplay rather than… well, rather than nothing at all, actually.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2977368894

Furthermore, unlike Phasmo, you have to earn the maps. You’ll start with a basic map, and the others are unlocked in stages as you level up. The same applies to certain items. This gives a sense of progression that Phasmo didn’t have before its latest update.

On top of that, there are various cosmetic items (clothes, locations and props) to buy, which adds a bit of customisation – and that’s quite welcome.

Now that you’ve found the ghost, can you just leave? Oh no, my dear lady…

You can exorcise it. To do so, you’ll have a short quest that varies from map to map; it’s generally not insurmountable in itself, but don’t forget that your sanity has been on the wane for quite some time now…

There are EVEN MORE quests per map – usually more like Easter eggs or nods to the game than anything else – but it shows there’s plenty to do.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2976926780

So is the game perfect?

Well, no – the game is in early access and still suffers from plenty of issues. No major bugs, but I can list a few:

- It’s sometimes REALLY ugly, and frankly it’s getting annoying because…
- … it’s also sometimes incredibly poorly optimised. I sometimes get FPS drops down to 20 in the middle of a match, for no reason. And this happens to everyone at the same time.
- The graphics glitch sometimes. No idea what causes it, but you’ll encounter graphical glitches, particularly with moving objects.
- Evidence glitches. A classic of the genre – you sometimes get a ghost painting a canvas that nobody else can see, or cameras that don’t transmit the footage, etc. It’s frustrating and, frankly, it can ruin the game.

You know what to expect, but there are regular updates and, to be honest, I never get bored of the game at all… It’s nothing like other games in the genre and is great fun to play with friends.

The game is great when all the mechanics want to work right. The atmosphere is creepy, the locations are all varied and interesting, and the tools are all unique plays on classic ghost hunting items. The animations of the characters are, for the most part, pretty good too. There’s some character customization, base upgrades, and decorations. The jump scares and events are varied and can be terrifying or interesting. There are even things in the environment that you can read aloud which will cause a little surprise which is pretty cool the first few times.

Now for the bad. The basic tools are all mostly good enough to figure out what kind of ghost you’re dealing with. The extras will help you complete the “optional objectives” which in turn will let you exorcise the ghost/demon. You most likely won’t be able to do that without buying some sort of extra tool like a candle or camera. But just one of those tools cost thousands and will require a little grinding/farming. But when you die and lose your extra tools, it really sets the game back due to just how expensive everything is; it feels extremely punishing when you die, and you will die especially while trying to learn the later exorcisms.

Some of the base items don’t seem to be very intuitive or seem to take forever to use. Fingerprints aren’t consistently seen with UV light. The ESG tool (DOTS) and the Easel (Ghost drawing/writing) seemingly take forever to work with no rhyme or reason as to when or why; some games have lasted 30+ minutes of just staring at these last two items hoping for an interaction for a final piece of ghost evidence. Your basic EMF tool is based upon distance of the item interacted with, but doesn't take into consideration if the item is thrown out of reach or in an entirely different room above or below you.

Now there is a bare bones written “how to play” tutorial that you can read, but it does little to really show you how to use each tool and when and why they’ll work.

There are 3 “cursed objects” in the game, but they feel like blatant and cheaper rip offs from another popular ghost hunting game. A ouija board that can only be asked 4 very specific questions with only one being useful. A voodoo doll that can either cause more activity or a hunt, and a tarot deck with cards that cause random effects.

There are 24 ghosts with different personalities, but they’re not very distinct and sometimes don’t even feel like they’re working right; there’s a ghost that angers when it hears cussing and swearing, but a hilarious game was spent doing that without any repercussions. One of the ghosts even has one of their attributes as "we have no data" as if the devs just gave up on adding anything.

Also you can’t complete your optional objects (like take a photo of the ghost or collect “item”) at the same time and while you’re looking for the ghost room and trying to figure out the ghost type. It seems like this is in place just to make you spend more time in the location instead of respecting the player’s time.

Difficulty wise, the game seems pretty balanced and almost too easy at times on “easy”, but if you bump up the difficulty, the ghost seems to interact less and less with its environment meaning you can’t get the evidence you need to ID it. It turns into a game of looking for a possible ghost room that hasn’t had anything happen in it, in the dark (since the lights will supposedly break more and more as you heighten the difficulty, even though some easy games, I’ve had literally every light break), and just walking around until you’re insane enough that the ghost will constantly hunt you. There is a custom mode, but the options are extremely limited and don’t seem very worth it since they’ll tank your money/reward multiplier. 

Each location has a very specific way to exorcise the ghost that won’t change and is always your last objective. All of these also involve running around the map, looking for some sort of object(s) that only spawn in once your optional objectives are done. Some of these, especially on earlier maps, require you to pick up “x” amount of an object (rats, fingers, etc.) and take them somewhere. This is made more frustrating because they count as a tool and you’ll only be able to carry up to 3 at most; they later change this in the later maps thankfully and let you pick up and hold all items at once. Currently, one of the more frustrating exorcisms involves finding an item that will only spawn in the map once you lock in your ghost type (right or wrong), which can spawn anywhere in the house, and also immediately starts a timer for another final part of the exorcism which involves you examining multiples bodies using vague instructions.

Some random low points. There’s no global talk (like a radio system), so don’t think of getting too far away from your friends. Your keybinds reset each and every time you quit the game. The ghosts don’t make noise when they’re hunting you, so it’s hard to pinpoint where they’re at or if they’re done. While you can use your flashlight at the same time as another tool, when you switch to that item to do so, your light turns off and you have to toggle it back on. The jump scares can get repetitive after a few hours (especially after grinding on a map for money) and have nothing to do with a particular ghost type or help in identifying it.

I’ll keep playing this game just to experience each map and unique exorcism puzzle, but afterwards, there’s no way I’m working my way up buying the penthouse base for $150,000. I really want to like this game more than I do, but the core mechanics just don’t feel consistent and the amount of time the game makes you waste in just constantly running around the map feels like it just doesn’t respect your time.

This game feels like it should still be in early access. Wait for a sale if you’re interested after trying the demo and have at least another person to play with. It feels like dev support had dropped off since they called it good and suddenly went out of early access.

When it comes to the gameplay, like most ghost hunting games, you just kind of wait around until your tools go off. I wish this game had a bit more to do or extra ways to identify the ghost in a more interactive way rather than sitting around in the correct room. After you play for a while you start to quickly understand how this game was developed and you can very easily cheese the mechanics in your favor. For example, the ghost listens to your microphone through the in-game chat system. Once you know the correct keywords to activate the ghost, identifying becomes quite easy and not challenging. You don't even need to ask its name or where it is. The game just hopes the user will YAP into their spirit box until they get scared and get hunted. The VERY scripted jump-scares also become quite laughable after the second time you encounter them. In terms of progression, there really is none. The character customization is also EXTREMELY limited. Barely any clothing to pick from and no unlockable outfits or skins based on level/progression.

I still have high hopes for this game as I think there is a lot of potential. I just think the developers need to really crack down and focus on this game.

The only reason I am currently playing is to farm a lot of money so that when new content DOES come out, although rarely, I can purchase it and play it.

My suggestions; Add daily, weekly, and monthly challenges that reward 'X' amount of money and XP. Please do NOT make them "Complete 'X' amount of matches on (INSERT MAP NAME)". Come up with creative challenges like completing a game in under 'X' amount of time or "correctly identify the ghost in (INSERT TIME FRAME). The steam store page advertises unique challenges but there are absolutely none, false advertising...

I also would like to see a progression overhaul, make customization options players would actually enjoy using such as unique clothing tied to your level, a prestige system which can unlock new cosmetics, trophies for your safehouses, skins for the various tools used to identify the ghosts, etc.

Overall, I hope this game gets the love it deserves. It has a HIGH amount of potential and I would love to see this game succeed. As of now, other ghost hunting games are superior because there is more content within them and progression has a bit more meaning.

In a game like this, I want to be able to learn about the ghost I am hunting, not see so many different ghosts all over the house when there is actually just one that really exists and the others are all just part of the furniture.

There are many aspects of Demonologist that are the exact same as Phas to a level that is not explainable other than copying. Just playing once, you will see it is set up exactly like Phas with only small changes.

Focusing on ghost type similarities, Poltergeists in folklore are said to throw objects as one of their main traits, so it makes sense both Phas and Demonologist have this the same. However, there are many ghosts in Demonologist that do not have an excuse for copying directly from Phas. One example being the Thaye. Thaye is just Burmese for ghost, and I could never find any indication of a link with aging in folklore, so I am certain the Phas devs created that unique aspect for the Thaye. Demonologist having the same information that a Thaye ages proves that it is not a coincidence and simply a blatant copy.

There are many more examples and an unsettling amount of ghosts that also appear in Phas. Speaking of "Ghosts", the game is called Demonologist but refers to the creatures as "ghosts" in game. There are specific demon names in the types as well, but also just a type called DEMON, so there is a serious lack of logic and originality in the "ghost" types as well.

I love the look of the old equipment and how everything else in game seems set back in time...until we pull out our tablet. The tablet is so out of place and ruins the older style of everything else. The tablet is also pulled out with "J" which makes no sense until you consider that in Phas, "J" is the default key for the "Journal". It feels as if Demonologist chose to make it a tablet only to differentiate itself a little from Phas but still left the keybind as "J" instead of making it "T" for tablet or anything else. It would be better off as a journal or something else not of a new technology to fit with the other equipment.

Something that struck me immediately as a red flag when first looking at the Steam page is the claim of "The best graphics in the co-op horror genre you'll ever play". I understand the game is in early access; most games I play on Steam are in early access. Most of my concerns with Demonologist are very core elements and are unlikely to be fixed, which is why I will be refunding and advising against this game. When dev teams take care in creating the game and updating it, even early access games can be amazing right away.

This leads to a large concern with the developer. In October 2021, less than a year and a half ago, Demonologists developer released Haunt Chaser. The game looks nice. The Unreal 5 engine really sells the look of the game in just a few pictures. Demonologist, at first, seems like the visual experience that us Phasmophobia players have been waiting for, and it is. The game play itself is less polished than Phasmo and is extremely minimal at its core. There are a few interesting things sprinkled here and there, but it's almost redundant.

The biggest issues here are 1) The scare factor and 2) the game play.

Someone on Steam reviewed Demonoligist and said something akin to:
“It's like a Disney ride where each time it's the same scares, but now you're looking for the little things that you might have missed.”
Which is the most accurate review on this game that I've read.

My first time playing Demonologist, we entered a house that (surprisingly) looked like the house from the game Edith Finch, with plenty of it's assets. They're free so it's almost expected. Immediately a yellow ghost appeared, floated at us and snorted like a pig loudly. 4 seconds later a small boy appeared, giggled and ran away as a loud noise spooked us. Moments later we noticed words like “Angry” and “Victoria” on paintings or walls and repeated them. To no one's surprise a loud noise triggered and a ghost ran through the room. These scares repeated over and over again. By our 3rd play through we were fatigued by the repeated loud noises. That is Demonologist's overall horror vibe. All of the scares are scripted and hard coded to each specific map. If you've played Phasmo, the scares are limited to the ghost appearing in 1 of a few fashions and occasionally light bulbs popping loudly. This means the scares can happen at any time, anywhere. Whereas in Demonologist you can expect to see the same scares most of the time, in the exact same places over and over again.

The next major issue is the game play. You can expect to grab your Cockroach-EMF hybrid device and thermometer and roam the level until one or the other gets a hit. This is what you will do Every Single Game. Unfortunately the ghost AI seems to be programmed to start interacting with the environment fairly early into your investigations. My friends and I have walked into rooms several times to witness bottles, books or picture frames being tossed across the room, thus ending our hunt for the ghost room sometimes 1 minute into the game. While this might be okay for less experienced ghost hunters, for me and my friends we found this a little too obvious and quick-paced which oddly becomes suddenly extremely slow paced. This pattern of:
[enter house > 4 loud jump scares > see books and bottles being thrown > setup gear]
quickly devolves into sitting for several minutes until another spectacular scare happens, all the while waiting for evidence to trigger. It's a strange concept to start with the volume cranked up to 11, then go down to 0. It should be reversed.

Demonologist also suffers from what I consider a strange design choice of linear-objective-based game play. Your first objective is to figure out what type of ghost is haunting the building. Your secondary objectives are randomized between a handful of tasks and your third objective is always to exercise the ghost. What's strange is that these objectives have to be solved in order. Meaning you cannot have some team mates in the ghost room trying to figure out what type of ghost you're dealing with while other players work on the secondary objectives at the same time. Your team must first unanimously agree on the ghost type. Only once you've all agreed the game spawns in the secondary objectives into the map. Oddly, once you've picked a ghost, you cannot change your selection and the game warns you so. If you've completed both objectives then you can exercise the ghost. This seems extremely arbitrary because as I've said earlier, you do a sizable amount of nothing sitting in the ghost room waiting for the Canvas, ESG or EMF to trigger, except getting jump scared. Why not allow others to complete the secondary objectives? Why force everyone to do nothing while sitting around waiting for the second or third and final evidence to be shown, when some players could choose to split up and have their own fun while completing side tasks? It really helps Phasmo shine a bit more compared to Demonologist when you look the gear selection and how little is involved in “setting up” any of it. You simply “drop” an ESG or Canvas, there is no setup button or placement button, or orientation rotation. You change your equipped item to a crucifix and just hold it to save yourself from a ghost attack, no need to place it down in order to prevent a hunt within a radius. UV lights are the same, you just equip them, no need to turn them on/off or “recharge” them by shaking. It's all a little dull.

There's also a camera system, but strangely the first and only camera you operate is pointing at your “base” (it's a big tent) and yields no benefit other than to say “Phasmo did it.” Sure you can buy and place additional cameras elsewhere, by what's the point of sitting outside at base and looking at your base on a screen? 

I'd like to see the maps expanded (they are beautiful.) Cyclone St basically screams Demonologist by having a living room wall demolished and showing a secret labyrinth beneath the home. It's a scary concept and could expand the replay value by having that area being “found” later on once the Sledgehammer is unlocked. Instead, much like the scares, the horror is shown upfront and early and and there isn't a whole lot more to it. Sure some bookcases move when you say the written word on one of the books, or a wall disappears magically when you repeat the word on a picture frame, but those are things that could be saved until a later play through and give you excitement to play the same map again. You'll be grinding the first map about 10 or 12 times before more become unlocked, so, why not?

In closing, the game looks great but plays “meh”. I'd like to see the maps get expanded, giving you reasons to revisit them over time. I'd like a little more interactivity with your gear. It'd be great if the scripted scares were reduced to only happening a small percentage of the time and/or when sanity is low. Or at least not immediately triggering upon entering the level. And a plethora of “general” scares that can be used across multiple maps rather than relying on the level designed to manually add the scary blueprints individually (this would also solve the silly notion of watching a picture frame or giant grandfather clock fall to the ground, then quietly float back up to it's starting animation and trigger again 30 seconds later.) I'd also like to see a simplified overhaul to the “Journal Tablet” UI as well as the removal of “pick ghost first before doing anything else” game play. There's some major connection issues (getting kicked mid game, losing mics mid-game, random crashes) that are in need of some TLC too.

I hope this game gets better, sooner rather than later. I got my monies worth, but I bought it on sale. And even that price can't bring me and my friends back to play this visually impressive but soul-less game.

Picked this up with some friends and initially it was promising, as we've spend a lot of time on Phasma and we're looking for something similar. 

Demonologist has a great concept in that it's phasma-and-then-some. After identifying the ghost / demon there is another game-stage where you can then 'banish' or exorcise the thing. All sounding good so far.

I always say that a game should be judged on its own merits, but Demonologist is so similar to Phasmaphobia that I cannot help but draw comparisons. I mean, the whole identifying the ghost stage is almost pound for pound the same. You have clues that help you narrow down the ghost-type, exactly the same like Freezing temps, Fingerprints, Spirit Box etc. but Demonologist has a couple of extra ones thrown in. Not an issue - I bought this because of it's similarities with Phasma.

However, the general concepts and ideas thrown into this game while ok, none are particularly executed very well.

The first (and only) level you're given access to when you first play I'd describe more as a house of horrors at a fun fair... there are 'set' jumpscares throughout the map - and these happen each and every time you play the map - they quickly become routine and expected and inevitably, dull. Moreover, the scares appear to have nothing to do with the 'ghost' at large.

For example, there is a picture in a hallway that shows a phrase with a missing word - the word is 'ball' and if you say into the mic the whole phrase, the set piece triggers and plays out ... Ok. I love the fact I can actually speak a phrase and something triggers in the game, but the fact that this exists each and every playthrough of the map, in exactly the same fashion makes me think it more of a gameplay concept - a bit like, "hey, look what this game can do, we can get the player to say something to trigger in-game events" - yeah that's cool, but how have they really implemented this into the gameplay? They haven't basically.

Compounding this, is that all these events has literally zero to-do with the ghost you're trying to identify - so what's the point of it? Sure, seeing it for the first time is impressive and I wondered what else was to come, as its not the only 'set piece' - but there is nothing more to it. There are a number of similar triggers dotted about the map that, while we played at least, became very routine to go around and trigger them all. Doing so does not move the investigation on, nor do you learn anything about the ghost... so in my opinion, there is no point to these events other than to dazzle your initial learning of them. A great gameplay concept, with no implementation into the 'real' gameplay loop at all.

Another large issue for me is that Ghosts all appear to behave the same. In Phasma there are very subtle differences in Ghost types, you need to play a good number of rounds to understand how subtle these differences can be. Demonologist doesn't appear to have this depth - along with the 'set scares' you also 'see' the ghost a times, and it'll chase you in a 'hunting phase' similar to Phasma. The ghost has no correlation to what you see. You'll see a old woman ghost one second, then a big fat demon thing the next, so you never really know what you're up against. Along with the set jumpscares, it all feels a bit random and as I said before 'funfair house of horrors' vibes - For a core gameplay 'draw' for me, it all feels poorly implemented. Just a bunch of ideas thrown into a pot and hope it all works.

Unlocking maps is painstakingly slow, and the only apparent mechanic to unlock these is to to grind the one map you have access to until you have enough in-game cash for the next map. This grind is unreasonably long, imo, and smarter 'blockers' should have been used to rather than some arbitrary in-game pay-wall. I mean, why? Why spend time creating maps that people may never unlock? A better system would be to have all maps available, and issues such as lack of proper equipment should 'block' the player from progressing - at least let them see what's in store in the higher echelons of the game. In the 5.3 hours I played so far I have unlocked ONE map. I'm not sorry to tell you, the gameplay loop is not even nearly strong enough for the time investment needed to unlock maps. If I return to this game after some updates, I can imagine myself loading it up, remembering 'oh yeah I only have two maps' and not even bothering to check the rest of the game because it's boring to play one / two maps, containing the same stuff, over and over.

A final note, as is a common problem with many Early Access games is simply lack of content. As far as I can see the game is being updated, piecemeal updates, a thing here, a thing there - y'know there is nothing wrong with this, and I celebrate the developers for continuing with updates - good - but there are fundamental issues with the game that will affect its longevity with the gameplay loop, the quickly-becoming-cheap set jumpscares and the map unlocks that must be resolved to order to change this thumbs down to a thumbs up.

Summary; In it's current state I'm not recommending - Phasmaphobia is early access, is doing what Demonologist is doing better and is currently cheaper - so Clock Wizard Games need to up their game. Literally.

Overall, this is really good. The ghost types are actually somewhat unique and can do interesting things, the equipment works about as reliably as you can hope for, it looks fine visually (though looking through a video camera drops the quality for some reason), and the maps are designed pretty well. There are also "secrets" on each map which are kinda neat even if they don't do anything, and having exorcism as a thing to do after identifying the ghost is a neat little feature. Same with having different safe houses you can customize a little. Nothing groundbreaking, but it's fun. I do find it scarier than Phasmo, partly for the jumpscares but also because sometimes the ghosts will say stuff to screw with you.

That said, there are definitely some downsides. 
-The cost of everything is *insane*. On easy for the first map, if you do all the objectives and the exorcism you'll get something like $1200 at most. You can buy a thermometer with that much...and that's it. Cameras are like $1600, crucifixes are $2000, it's way too much. If you want the Big Bucks you gotta do higher difficulties, but if you die, you lose the equipment and getting money takes so long that losing a single piece just completely screws you, so I really think the costs need to be lowered just a little. 
-There aren't that many kinds of equipment, the ones present are fine but there really could be more like sound or motion sensors, parabolic mics, maybe remote temperature sensors.
-The ghosts being so unique kinda works against it. If something randomly vanishes from your hands or the tripod camera teleports then you automatically know it's a Naamah without having to do a single thing since they're the only ghost that steals your stuff. Same with a Yokai, if it hunts within the first few minutes when you have like 80% sanity you know it's a Yokai for sure because they're guaranteed to hunt at a specific time.
-It's heavy on the jumpscares which is neat but they get old after a while.
-The presence of character customization is cool but there aren't many options

It's really good for what it is, just play it yourself before you check out the community hub. For some reason, the hub has a lot of weird people ranting about how the game has been "abandoned" because it hasn't had an update since September (there's a single dev apparently, plus Phasmo also goes months without major content updates and even if it has the game is fully playable as is), it's "full of bugs" (I'm sure they exist but I've literally only ever encountered a single noteworthy bug), the equipment "never works" (I've literally never had this be a problem, at least not any more than Phasmo), it's a "scam" because of the above points, etc. so play it yourself and see but I think it's a good time.

Edit: found a new downside. Gonna be real, the writing is....not great. There are some notes, usually with general lore, and they're not unreadable at all but I think having someone edit them for clarity would be very helpful, especially the ones related to the side quest. The quest itself is neat, I hope they make more of them but the writing is not very good both in terms of the readability of the notes and the actual story itself. I really think having someone proofread the notes and quest stories would go a long way. There's so much potential but it needs some work.
